newsitem.title: UK: PRESS DIGEST - British business press - March 7.
newsitem.headline: PRESS DIGEST - British business press - March 7.

text.p: Prepared for Reuters by The Broadcast Monitoring Company
DAILY TELEGRAPH
-- SHARES BLAZE A TRAIL ACROSS EUROPE

Share prices across Europe rose to record levels yesterday, pushed on by corporate profits, a firm Wall Street and probability of interest rates remaining unchanged for the immediate future. In London, the results from the latest Confederation of British Industry survey on consumer spending, which suggests that high street spending is slowing down also lifted the mood of investors.The FT-SE index of 100 leading shares leapt 39.2 points to a record 4399.3. The Dax index in Frankfurt rose 1.56 per cent to a record 3,417.60 and the Paris CAC index reached a record of 2,700.43 up 1.28 per cent.
-- JOHN LEWIS STAFF SHARE 82 MILLION POUNDS BONANZA

John Lewis, the department store and supermarket group, yesterday announced a taxable profit up 45 per cent to 217 million last year. The Partnership then revealed that its 37,000 employees would share a staff bonus of 82 million pounds stg. The bonus is worth about 10 weeks' pay for full and part-time staff, with all employees from chairman down, receiving it.
-- REGULATOR WILL PROBE CENTRICA PRICE CUTTING

Gas regulator, Clare Spottiswoode yesterday launched an urgent inquiry into whether Centrica, the newly demerged British Gas GAS.L trading business, should be prevented from offering selective price cuts to direct debit customers in South-west England. The move follows strong complaints from rival suppliers. Miss Spottiswoode said she had not sanctioned the move and that she was concerned the cuts on offer could stifle competition.
THE TIMES -- TREASURY ATTACKED OVER POWER SHARES SALE DECISION

A Commons committee yesterday criticised Treasury officials for the failure to alert ministers to price sensitive information in the run-up to the sale of a second tranche of electricity generating companies shares. The report from the Committee of Public Accounts, criticised the officials for not informing them of an impending price review by Stephen Littlechild, the electricity industry watchdog, which was announced the day after stock market trading began in the partly paid shares of National Power and PowerGen.
BTR CUTS PAYOUT AS EARNINGS FALL 13 PER CENT

BTR said yesterday that it is confident of completing its restructuring programme by the end of this year. The diversified industrial company expects to sell a further 25 non-core businesses to reach a target of total sales of 2.3 billion pounds stg, including 1.75 billion pounds stg in disposals last year. The disposal programme, as well as a poor performance in the automotive division led to a 13 per cent fall in full year pre- tax profits to 1.3 billion pounds stg. -- R-R PUSHED INTO RED BY 263 MILLION POUNDS SPECIAL CHARGE

An exceptional charge of 263 million pounds stg relating to its steam power generation division pushed Rolls Royce to a 28 million pounds stg pre-tax loss last year. Parsons Power Generation and International combustion, the business involved, is up for sale and Rolls Royce are confident a buyer will be found, with Siemens and GEC both thought to be interested. Earnings before exceptionals was up to 12.7p a share from 7.94p.
THE GUARDIAN
-- PEARSON CLOSES STABLE DOOR

Pearson has offered its employees a 30-day amnesty to report control failures in it's global empire. The move is an attempt to stamp out any more "black holes" such as the 100 million pounds stg loss uncovered at its Penguin subsidiary last month. The Pearson management is concerned that any further embarrassments may harm market confidence and undermine attempts to restructure the company.
-- HIGH STREET SPENDING SLOWS DOWN

Figures published yesterday by the Confederation of British Industry reveal that high street sales slowed down in February. Half of the retailers interviewed saw sales rise and just under a quarter reported sales down. Consumers are being more careful about how they spend their money and will shop around to make sure they are getting the best price and value, said Alastair Eperon, the chairman of the CBI distributive trades survey panel.
-- BA TARGETS SUPERJUMBO

British Airways has confirmed that it is interested in buying the Superjumbo jet expected to be launched by Airbus Industrie next year. Nineteen airlines have now expressed an interest in the A3XX Superjumbo which will carry around 900 passengers and will be able to fly non-stop between Europe and Australia. BA, although having put no money into the 5 billion pounds stg project, is discussing with Airbus the kind of specifications it would require if it made a commitment to place an order for the aircraft.
THE INDEPENDENT
-- GLAXO CALMS FEARS OVER LOSS OF ZANTAC PATENT

Glaxo Wellcome yesterday moved to allay fears in the City about its future, when its best-selling anti-ulcer drug loses partial patent protection in the US later this year. The drug accounted for almost a quarter of the group sales last year. Sir Richard Sykes, the chief executive warned that sales of Zantac could fall by up to 80 per cent but gave a clear message to analysts that he expected turnover growth to be back up in double digit percentages by 1999, with earnings at least being maintained over the next two years.
-- NOMURA CLAIMS TOKYO DIRECTORS 'SIPHONED FUNDS'

Nomura Securities yesterday announced that it suspected that two of its directors in Tokyo had conducted unauthorised trades to the benefit of a client's account. The announcement came after the Tokyo market had closed, but the news was greeted with shock in London where shares in Nomura, the biggest stockbroker in the world, plummeted by 9 per cent.
-- RAILTRACK AND FREIGHT LOBBY CLASH OVER 16 BILLION POUNDS
PLAN

Freight operators yesterday attacked Railtrack's plan to spend 16 billion pounds stg over the next ten years on Britain's rail network, saying that they were dismayed by the lack of detail in the plans. In a letter to the Rail Regulator, the Rail Freight Group, which represents 150 freight operators, complained that Railtrack's forecasts gave little technical information and virtually nothing of interest to the freight industry.
